title: HInT: Hypergraph Infusion at the Structural Layers Improves Table Understanding
claim: Graph-augmented methods fail to consistently beat a simple fine-tuned text-only baseline, motivating a better way to inject structure.
layout: 1 panel, grouped bars over 3 datasets, legend on top
description: A single grouped bar chart compares six models on three table-reasoning benchmarks: WikiTQ, HiTab and TabFact. The y-axis is Accuracy, running from 40 to about 85, with dotted gridlines at 60 and 80. A two-row legend across the top lists Qwen2.5-3B in gray, Qwen2.5-3B (SFT) in yellow, HeGTa in blue, LLaSA in teal and TaMo in beige. In each dataset group the gray base model is far lower. The yellow SFT bar is as tall as or taller than the graph-based bars (blue, teal and beige). The eye goes first to the gray bar sitting well below the others. It then goes to the yellow bar topping each group, which shows that prior graph methods add little over plain fine-tuning. HInT is not shown.
caption: Comparison of text-only and graph-augmented LLMs
abstract: Decoder-only large language models (LLMs) struggle with table reasoning because tables must be serialized, which can obscure row- and column-level structure. Prior graph and hypergraph approaches encode structure with an external encoder, but their gains are often inconsistent under autoregressive decoding. We analyze how tabular structure is represented inside decoder-only LLMs and find that row and column relations are concentrated in a small subset of layers and attention heads. Based on this observation, we propose HInT ( H ypergraph In fusion for T able reasoning), which injects hypergraph-derived structural features directly into the layers where these relations are concentrated. HInT constructs a table hypergraph over cells and headers, applies lightweight message passing, and fuses the resulting structural features with token hidden states through gated fusion. Experiments across diverse table reasoning tasks show consistent improvements over text-only baselines and prior (hyper)graph-based methods.
